This is the NEAREST plant, not the SERVING plant — compare with sewer_service_area_provider; when the two differ, the point is nearer to one plant than to the one its wastewater is modeled to reach.
fields.name: nearest_wastewater_plant_name
fields.null_meaning: No CWNS 2022 wastewater treatment plant within 50 km, the nearest plant carries no usable facility name, or the local index is unavailable (bootstrap-pending / corrupt asset).

fields.description: Residential population served by the nearest wastewater treatment plant per CWNS 2022, including population from upstream collection systems that discharge into it. A measure of plant scale, not spare capacity.
fields.interpretation_hints: Residential population served by the nearest plant per CWNS 2022, INCLUDING population from upstream collection systems that discharge into it — the honest measure of plant scale, since a large regional plant's directly-served count is near zero by construction. Nationally the median plant serves ~1,500 people (p25 476, p75 6,353, p90 25,654, max 3.35 M), so this is the field that distinguishes a village lagoon from a regional facility. It is SCALE, NOT SPARE CAPACITY: it says nothing about headroom for a new industrial or data-center load — that is a phone call to the operator. Actual (as-operated) flow is not in CWNS at all; it lives in NPDES/ECHO. The figure excludes nonresidential/industrial load. A value of 0 means the plant reported no residential population — which can mean it treats purely industrial or reuse flow, or that the figure was left at zero; CWNS does not distinguish these, and 411 of 17,687 plants report 0. Review status varies by tier: every figure is self-reported through a state survey coordinator, and for roughly 1,200 plants the state confirmed only that the plant exists without gathering any technical data at all. Read with sewer_service_area_provider and public_water_system_population_served.
fields.name: nearest_wastewater_plant_population_served
fields.null_meaning: No CWNS 2022 wastewater treatment plant within 50 km, or the local index is unavailable (bootstrap-pending / corrupt asset). A plant that reported zero residential population returns 0, not null.

fields.description: Geodesic distance to the nearest mapped EPA CWS service-area polygon edge; 0.0 when the point is already inside one; null beyond the 50 km search cap.
fields.interpretation_hints: Straight-line geodesic distance to the nearest mapped CWS service-area EDGE: 0.0 when the point is already inside one (i.e. within_water_service_area is True), otherwise the true edge distance up to 50,000 m; null beyond that means "no mapped service area within 50 km" — not zero, not unknown. It is a screening proxy only — NOT pipe-route distance, NOT a main-extension cost estimate, and NOT evidence a utility will extend service (that is a will-serve decision about capacity and annexation). Roughly 43% of EPA boundaries are ml_modeled, so an edge distance is measured against a statistical estimate as often as not — always read with water_service_area_provenance. Independent of the name/provenance fields (it populates even outside any service area). Pair with nearest_sewer_service_area_distance_m for a combined wet-utility screen.
fields.name: nearest_water_service_area_distance_m
fields.null_meaning: No mapped CWS service-area polygon edge falls within the 50 km search cap (a deep-rural / backcountry / offshore coordinate), or the local CWS index is unreadable.

fields.description: How the containing CWS service-area boundary was obtained — utility_sourced (state agency/utility/public GIS submission) or ml_modeled (EPA machine-learning estimate).
fields.interpretation_hints: How the containing service-area boundary was obtained: utility_sourced = published by a state/utility/public-GIS source (high evidentiary weight); ml_modeled = an EPA machine-learning estimate (Random Forest, Decision Tree, parcel or OpenStreetMap derivation) — 43% of all polygons — whose edge is a statistical guess and never equal in precision to a sourced boundary. NEVER infer this from geography or from how well-known the utility is: Baton Rouge Water Company (580,000 people served), Lansing Board of Water & Light and Augusta-Richmond County are all ml_modeled, while much smaller systems are utility_sourced. Gate every confident claim about within_water_service_area, water_system_name and nearest_water_service_area_distance_m on this field. Same vocabulary as sewer_service_area_provenance, so the two are directly comparable.
fields.name: water_service_area_provenance
fields.null_meaning: within_water_service_area is False. Also null in three rarer cases, each named in the field's notes — the containing polygon's provenance cell is blank upstream, the upstream value is one this API does not map (logged as schema drift and never passed through raw), or the published CWS artifact predates the provenance column (a pre-V3.0 edition, expected for one restart during a rebuild publish).

fields.description: Geodesic distance to the nearest underground-storage-tank facility in EPA's UST Finder national composite (open or closed tanks); null beyond the 8 km screening band.
fields.interpretation_hints: Geodesic distance to the nearest underground-storage-tank facility in EPA's UST Finder national composite (689,673 facilities served, searched within an 8 km screening band). A REGISTERED TANK FACILITY IS NOT CONTAMINATION — 72% of these facilities have only closed tanks, and most never had a release; this is a former-fuel-retail / land-use-legacy signal and a due-diligence prompt, not a measurement of soil or groundwater impact. The contamination signal in this family is open_lust_sites_within_1km_count. The data is a FROZEN SNAPSHOT — states as of 2018-2019, territories 2020-2021, tribal lands as of October 2025 — so a tank installed or removed since is absent, and EPA's UST Finder 2.0 re-standardization is pending. About two-thirds of facility positions are geocoded from a street address rather than surveyed, so treat this as a screening-scale figure that locates a RECORD OF A FACILITY, not a tank or a dispenser island. Read with nearest_superfund_distance_m, nearest_brownfield_distance_m and nearest_rcra_tsd_distance_m, which use the same 8 km band.
fields.name: nearest_ust_facility_distance_m
fields.null_meaning: No UST Finder facility within 8 km (a semantic absence), or the local index is unavailable (bootstrap-pending / corrupt asset).

fields.description: Exact count of EPA UST Finder underground-storage-tank facilities within 1 km — a density signal for historical fuel-retail and fleet-fueling land use, not a contamination count.
fields.interpretation_hints: Exact count of UST Finder tank facilities within 1 km — a density signal for historical fuel-retail and fleet-fueling land use. 1 KM IS DELIBERATELY NARROW: at the 8 km band the other contaminated-site fields use, this count runs into the thousands in any city (1,489 in downtown Houston) and stops being a signal. For reference, ASTM E1527-21 requires only property and adjoining properties for registered-UST records, so 1 km is considerably more inclusive than standard due diligence. Zero means none within 1 km, not none in the area — most non-urban coordinates return 0, and 0 is a real answer at ok status, never a missing value. Counts can still be inflated where a state supplied ONE coordinate for many records: centroid-grade positions (postal and locality geocodes) are excluded from the served index, but 8.6% of remaining rows share a coordinate with another facility, and the worst such stack carries 97 state-supplied rows. Read with open_lust_sites_within_1km_count, which is the contamination half of the pair.
fields.name: ust_facilities_within_1km_count
fields.null_meaning: The local index is unavailable (bootstrap-pending / corrupt asset); a successful empty radius returns 0.

fields.description: Exact count of leaking-underground-storage-tank (LUST) release sites within 1 km whose state cleanup status reads Open in EPA's UST Finder snapshot.
fields.interpretation_hints: Exact count of leaking-UST release sites within 1 km whose state cleanup status reads OPEN — releases still being monitored or remediated, not the 84% of historical releases already closed out. THIS IS THE CONTAMINATION SIGNAL IN THIS FAMILY, and 1 km is slightly more inclusive than ASTM E1527-21's 0.5-mile (805 m) minimum search distance for state leaking-tank databases. Cleanup status is AS REPORTED IN THE 2018-2021 SNAPSHOT, not current, so a release closed out since then may still read as open and a release opened since is absent — confirm current status with the state agency before relying on it. Zero means none within 1 km, and is a real answer at ok status, never a missing value. Read with ust_facilities_within_1km_count and the Superfund / brownfield / RCRA-TSD proximity fields; THESE COUNTS ARE PER-PROGRAM AND OVERLAP BY DESIGN — one physical site can appear as a UST facility, an open LUST release and an ACRES brownfield, so they must not be summed.
fields.name: open_lust_sites_within_1km_count
fields.null_meaning: The local index is unavailable (bootstrap-pending / corrupt asset); a successful empty radius returns 0.

fields.description: True if the queried point falls inside a USGS-mapped area of karst or pseudokarst — rock units that have developed, or have the potential to develop, dissolution or collapse features including sinkholes, caves and lava tubes.
fields.interpretation_hints: An area SCREEN, not a susceptibility or collapse-probability rating — USGS states explicitly that these maps "do not indicate degrees of karst hazards within the areas depicted, such as susceptibility for sinkhole collapse", and that areas of significant karst hazard are only a small subset of what is delineated. About 13.5% of random points in the lower 48 fall inside a mapped unit, so True is common and is a prompt for site-specific investigation, never a finding. True also includes PSEUDOKARST (basaltic lava tubes, piping cavities in loose sediment, thermokarst in ice-rich permafrost) — read karst_type to know which mechanism. True likewise includes DEEPLY BURIED soluble rock: read karst_exposure_class, because a buried_ value can mean carbonate under up to ~90 m of insoluble cover with no surface expression at all. Source map units are generally 1:500,000 scale or smaller and USGS's own downstream use buffers them by 1 km, so a False within ~1 km of a mapped boundary is not a safe negative — which is why False reads medium confidence rather than high. Mapped coverage is the 50 states plus Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, but a small tail of polygons lies outside the served coordinate envelope and is unreachable in practice: units south of 18.0 latitude (the southern Puerto Rico coast and USVI), east of -65.0 longitude (USVI), and the western Aleutians across the antimeridian. The compilation is a static 2014 product and is not updated as state geologic maps are revised.
fields.name: in_karst_area

fields.description: Which ground-collapse mechanism the containing map unit represents — one of carbonate, evaporite, sandstone_solution, volcanic_pseudokarst, piping_pseudokarst or thermokarst.
fields.interpretation_hints: The mechanism behind in_karst_area, which matters because the six values carry very different engineering implications. carbonate (90,300 of the 112,162 mapped units) is limestone/dolostone/marble dissolution — the classic sinkhole mechanism. evaporite (8,220) is gypsum or halite, which dissolves far faster than carbonate and can collapse on engineering rather than geologic timescales; it is the most aggressive value here. sandstone_solution (16 units, in Minnesota only) is quartz sandstone with solution features. volcanic_pseudokarst (11,738) is basaltic lava tubes — roof collapse WITHOUT dissolution. piping_pseudokarst (1,586, mostly Texas, South Dakota and Kansas) is subsurface erosion cavities in loose sediment. thermokarst (302, mapped exclusively in Alaska) is ground-ice thaw subsidence, which is progressive settlement rather than sudden collapse. Where mapped units OVERLAP, the value reported is the one that dissolves fastest, because that mechanism governs the shorter timescale: measured on the served artifact, 29 of 4,000 sampled points inside karst fall in more than one unit and 23 of those carry a type conflict — every one of them carbonate versus evaporite, which resolves to evaporite. Derived from the source LAYER, not from the upstream free-text KARST_TYPE sentence, which is absent entirely from the Alaska thermokarst layer and carries encoding damage elsewhere.
fields.name: karst_type
fields.null_meaning: in_karst_area is False — no mapped karst or pseudokarst unit at the point.

fields.description: How deeply the soluble rock is buried — one of exposed, buried_under_insoluble_cover, buried_under_thin_glacial_cover or buried_under_thick_glacial_cover.
fields.interpretation_hints: The single most load-bearing qualifier on in_karst_area. exposed (79,886 of the 112,162 mapped units) means soluble rock at or near the land surface — the sinkhole-relevant case. buried_under_insoluble_cover (1,806) means under less than 300 ft (~90 m) of insoluble sediments. buried_under_thin_glacial_cover (11,160) means under 50 ft (~15 m) or less of glacially derived insoluble sediments, and buried_under_thick_glacial_cover (5,400) means more than 50 ft of it. A buried_ value means the soluble unit is present at DEPTH but has little or no surface expression, and that distinction is the whole point of this field: Ames, Iowa reports in_karst_area true with buried_under_thick_glacial_cover, which is a completely different site condition from Bowling Green, Kentucky's exposed, and no other field in the set separates them. confidence follows this field — exposed reads high, any buried_ value reads low, and pseudokarst or a missing exposure attribute reads medium. This is a mapped burial CLASS, not a measured depth to rock; for a measured depth see bedrock_depth_cm.
fields.name: karst_exposure_class
fields.null_meaning: in_karst_area is False; or the containing unit is pseudokarst (volcanic, piping or thermokarst — surface features by definition, so the source carries no exposure attribute); or the containing unit is one of the 284 Hawaii carbonate units whose exposure attribute is blank upstream.

fields.description: Geodesic distance in metres to the nearest documented unplugged orphaned oil or gas well in the USGS DOW dataset, searched within a 50 km screening band. Covers 27 states only.
fields.interpretation_hints: Geodesic distance to the nearest DOCUMENTED unplugged orphaned oil or gas well in the USGS DOW dataset (117,672 wells across 27 states), searched within a 50 km screening band. Coverage is the first thing to check: 23 states, the District of Columbia and all territories have no inventory in this dataset, so a null here can mean 'nobody has looked' rather than 'nothing is near' — read documented_orphaned_wells_within_1km_count, which is null in the uninventoried case and 0 in an inventoried one. Even a NON-null distance can under-report in an uninventoried state, where the nearest documented well is necessarily across a state line and the true nearest well may be much closer; the provenance note says so when that applies. 'Documented' is load-bearing: the dataset lists only wells a state agency has already recorded with a known location, and the national undocumented population is estimated in the hundreds of thousands, far larger. USGS performed no well-by-well location verification and publishes no positional-accuracy metadata; Kansas and Montana coordinates (5,698 wells, 4.8% of the dataset) were derived by USGS from Public Land Survey System section descriptors — section-grade, and a section is one square mile — so treat this as a screening-scale figure, not a sub-100 m measurement. The dataset is a frozen edition published in August 2022, built from state source files spanning July 2019 to June 2022, and the ground truth moves in BOTH directions: $4.675 billion of Bipartisan Infrastructure Law money has been plugging wells since October 2022, so a listed well may already be plugged, and states are still documenting new ones. Read with nearest_superfund_distance_m and nearest_brownfield_distance_m for the wider contamination-screen picture.
fields.name: nearest_documented_orphaned_well_distance_m
fields.null_meaning: Either the state is not one of the 27 states inventoried by the USGS DOW dataset — read documented_orphaned_wells_within_1km_count, which is also null in that case and 0 when the state IS inventoried — or the state is inventoried and no documented orphaned well lies within 50 km, or the coordinate is not within a US state, or the local index is unavailable (bootstrap-pending / corrupt asset).

fields.description: Exact count of documented unplugged orphaned oil and gas wells within 1 km of the queried point, from the USGS DOW dataset. A 0 and a null mean different things — null means the state has no inventory in this dataset at all.
fields.interpretation_hints: Exact count of documented unplugged orphaned wells within 1 km — the site-adjacency band, chosen because the coordinates are not accurate enough to support a tighter one (4.8% of them are Public Land Survey System section-grade, and a section is one square mile). Nationally 99.5% of random points return 0 and 70% of points inside a producing region still return 0, so a non-zero count is a strong signal: legacy oil districts return tens to hundreds (44 at Bradford PA, 65 at Bolivar NY, up to 473 in the Allegany field). A 0 and a null mean completely different things here: 0 means this state's inventory was searched and nothing is within 1 km; null means the state has no inventory in this dataset at all, which is a coverage gap and NOT evidence that the state holds no orphaned wells (23 states, the District of Columbia and all territories are uninventoried, several of them with real oil-and-gas history). This is a screening prompt, not a liability determination — an orphaned well near a site is a due-diligence lead (methane leakage, plugging cost, groundwater risk, physical obstruction, access and title questions), and the responsible party, plugging status and state-program queue must be confirmed with the state oil-and-gas agency named in the release. Read with nearest_documented_orphaned_well_distance_m.
fields.name: documented_orphaned_wells_within_1km_count
fields.null_meaning: The state is not one of the 27 states inventoried by the USGS DOW dataset (a semantic absence — NOT a count of zero), the coordinate is not within a US state, or the local index is unavailable (bootstrap-pending / corrupt asset, including the state-coverage index that decides which of those applies). An inventoried state with no documented orphaned well within 1 km returns 0, not null.

fields.description: Modelled self-supplied (private-well) households per km², averaged over the 3 km × 3 km neighbourhood containing the point. USGS downscales a 2020 census-block self-supplied/publicly-supplied classification to a 1 km grid. Conterminous US only.
fields.interpretation_hints: Modelled self-supplied (private-well) HOUSEHOLDS per km², averaged over the 3 km × 3 km neighbourhood containing the point (3×3 cells of the source's 1 km equal-area grid) — a screening signal for how groundwater-dependent an area is: high density means neighbours draw their own groundwater, so there is no public water main, and a large new groundwater withdrawal carries drawdown, permitting and community-opposition exposure. This is a MODEL estimate, not a well inventory: a machine-learning classifier labels each 2020 census block self-supplied or publicly supplied and downscales to a 1 km grid, so it supports area screening but cannot confirm that any particular well exists at or near the point. HOUSEHOLDS, NOT WELLS — one household may have one well, and one well may serve several. DOMESTIC USE ONLY: irrigation, industrial and public-supply groundwater withdrawals are NOT counted, so this is not a measure of total aquifer competition, which for a large water user is usually dominated by exactly those uses. Screening-scale and area-describing, never parcel-level. Fixed 2020 vintage; conterminous US only, so Alaska, Hawaii and the territories are absent. A covered area with no self-supplied households returns 0.0, not null — that is the normal reading inside a city. Read with within_water_service_area (its complement: a public water-service area is where this should be near zero) and with nearest_groundwater_well_depth_to_water_m (a sparse USGS monitoring reading over a different well population).
fields.name: domestic_well_households_per_km2
fields.null_meaning: The point is outside the modelled product's coverage (it is conterminous-US only, so Alaska, Hawaii and the territories are absent, as are open ocean and points across the Canadian or Mexican border), or the local index is unavailable (bootstrap-pending / corrupt asset). A covered area with no self-supplied households returns 0.0, not null.

fields.description: Coarse class over the same modelled self-supplied-household density — none / sparse / moderate / dense / very_dense. Frozen physical bands, not quantiles.
fields.interpretation_hints: The same modelled value as domestic_well_households_per_km2, banded so it reads without a units lookup. Bands (households/km², frozen physical breaks, never quantiles — quantile breaks would bake any input bias into the labels): none = exactly 0.0; sparse = above 0 up to 1; moderate = above 1 up to 10; dense = above 10 up to 50; very_dense = above 50. Nationally about 41% of covered cells are none, 65% none-or-sparse, 92% at or below moderate, and above 50 is under 0.05% of covered area. `none` means the MODEL estimates no self-supplied households in the neighbourhood — not a guarantee that no well exists there. Every caveat on domestic_well_households_per_km2 applies unchanged: it is a model estimate rather than a well inventory, it counts households rather than wells, and it counts DOMESTIC use only (no irrigation, industrial or public-supply withdrawals). The class is absent exactly when the density is absent — the two never disagree about whether there is an answer.
fields.name: domestic_well_household_density_class
fields.null_meaning: The point is outside the modelled product's coverage (conterminous-US only, so Alaska, Hawaii, the territories, open ocean and points across the Canadian or Mexican border are absent), or the local index is unavailable (bootstrap-pending / corrupt asset). The class is absent exactly when domestic_well_households_per_km2 is absent; a covered area with no self-supplied households returns the class `none`, not null.

fields.description: CAL FIRE (Office of the State Fire Marshal) regulatory Fire Hazard Severity Zone class at the queried point: Moderate, High, Very High, or Non-Wildland. California-only; null outside California and on Federal Responsibility Area land, which CAL FIRE does not zone.
fields.interpretation_hints: CAL FIRE's regulatory Fire Hazard Severity Zone at the point — Moderate, High, Very High, or Non-Wildland — from the Office of the State Fire Marshal's own statewide maps (SRA map dated 29 September 2023, effective 1 April 2024; LRA map dated 24 March 2025). ALWAYS read it with fire_hazard_responsibility_area, because that field decides what this one legally means, and the two conventions are opposites. In SRA (state-protected land) all three hazard classes ARE the statutory zone under Public Resources Code 4201-4204 and no local government can override them. In LRA (incorporated cities and most other non-state land) only **Very High** carries statutory weight — Chapter 7A building code, defensible-space enforcement, and Civil Code 1103 natural-hazard disclosure — while LRA Moderate and High are informational model output and are NOT a regulatory trigger; treating an LRA "High" as a code trigger is the single easiest mistake to make with this field. Non-Wildland is a real classification (urban core, agriculture, low-fuel flats), not missing data. The statewide LRA layer is CAL FIRE's RECOMMENDATION: a city or county may adopt an ordinance EXPANDING the Very High extent and may never shrink it, so a "not Very High" LRA answer is a FLOOR, not a guarantee — check the jurisdiction's own adopted FHSZ map before treating a parcel as clear. THIS IS A CALIFORNIA-ONLY FIELD: outside California it is null because the product does not exist there, never because there is no wildfire hazard. A null INSIDE California is usually Federal Responsibility Area land — national forest, national park, BLM or DoD — which CAL FIRE has no statutory mandate to zone, so some of California's highest-hazard landscapes resolve absent here; absence is a jurisdiction artifact, NOT a finding of low hazard. This is a hazard-ZONE classification and nothing more — it is not a fire-risk score, not an insurance eligibility or rating determination, and not a defensible-space or Chapter 7A compliance check. Pair it with wildfire_annual_frequency (FEMA National Risk Index annualized wildfire frequency) for the modelled-frequency half of the picture.
fields.name: fire_hazard_severity_zone_class
fields.null_meaning: Null in three distinguishable cases, told apart by the field's status plus its provenance note. ABSENT / outside California: CAL FIRE FHSZ is a California-only regulatory product and does not apply — this is "not applicable", never "no wildfire hazard". ABSENT / inside California with no polygon in either the SRA or the LRA layer: predominantly Federal Responsibility Area land (national forest, national park, BLM, DoD), which CAL FIRE has no statutory mandate to zone, or an unclassified low-fuel pocket — again NOT a finding of low hazard. FAILED: the CAL FIRE query errored, only one of the two layers could be reached and it returned nothing, or the feature carried an FHSZ code outside the published vocabulary — i.e. no answer was obtained and a retry may help.

fields.description: Which wildfire-protection responsibility area the queried point falls in — SRA (state, CAL FIRE-protected) or LRA (local). Determines whether the accompanying fire_hazard_severity_zone_class is statutory in all classes (SRA) or only at Very High (LRA). California-only.
fields.interpretation_hints: SRA or LRA — who holds wildfire-protection responsibility at the point, and therefore how much legal weight fire_hazard_severity_zone_class carries. SRA (State Responsibility Area, CAL FIRE-protected) means the FHSZ class is unconditionally authoritative: all of Moderate, High and Very High are the statutory zone under Public Resources Code 4201-4204 and there is no local override. LRA (Local Responsibility Area — incorporated cities and most other non-state land) means the class is CAL FIRE's RECOMMENDATION under Government Code 51175-51189: only Very High is statutory there, and the local jurisdiction may have adopted an ordinance EXPANDING the Very High extent beyond the statewide map (expansion is legal, reduction is not). Always read with fire_hazard_severity_zone_class; the two are always taken from the SAME source polygon, so they can never describe different places. A THIRD regime exists and is deliberately NOT reported here: Federal Responsibility Area (national forest, national park, BLM, DoD), where CAL FIRE has no zoning mandate at all — an FRA point is null on BOTH fields, which is a jurisdiction artifact and NOT a finding of low hazard. This names the fire-protection JURISDICTION, not the fire department that would actually roll on a call; mutual-aid and contract-county arrangements are outside this dataset. CALIFORNIA-ONLY: null outside California means not applicable, not unprotected. Vintages: SRA map dated 29 September 2023 (effective 1 April 2024), LRA map dated 24 March 2025.
fields.name: fire_hazard_responsibility_area
fields.null_meaning: Null in the same three cases as fire_hazard_severity_zone_class and for the same reasons. ABSENT / outside California (CAL FIRE responsibility areas are a California construct). ABSENT / inside California with no SRA or LRA polygon, which in practice means Federal Responsibility Area land — a real third regime this field does not report, not missing data. FAILED: the CAL FIRE query errored or could not be completed. A null here never means the point is unprotected.

fields.description: Geodesic distance in metres from the queried point to the BOUNDARY of the nearest CAL FIRE FRAP historical wildfire perimeter (Firep25_1, 23,334 perimeters covering fires 1878 through 2025). Exactly 0 when the point is inside a recorded perimeter. The search is capped at 8,000 m; beyond that the field is absent, meaning "no recorded perimeter within 8,000 m", not "no fire nearby". California-only.
fields.interpretation_hints: Geodesic metres from the point to the nearest CAL FIRE FRAP historical wildfire perimeter's BOUNDARY, read live from CAL FIRE's own published perimeter layer (Firep25_1, released April 2026, 23,334 perimeters, fires 1878 through 2025). A value of exactly 0 means the point falls INSIDE a recorded perimeter. READ THE THREE COMPLETENESS FACTS BEFORE YOU READ THE NUMBER, because a false "no burn" is the expensive error with this dataset. FIRST, below-threshold fires are simply absent by design: CAL FIRE's own stated collection criteria are perimeters of 10 acres or more in timber, 50 acres or more in brush, or 300 acres or more in grass, and/or 3 or more impacted residential or commercial structures, and/or 1 or more fatality, with all cooperating agencies submitting at 10 acres or more — a small fire that burned this exact parcel and cleared none of those gates was never collected at all. SECOND, coverage depends on voluntary agency submission, and CAL FIRE states outright that fires are missing because historical records were lost or damaged, documentation was inadequate, or they "have not yet been incorporated into the database" — the gaps are real and are not uniformly distributed across counties, eras or agencies. THIRD, the current fire season is always missing: a season is published in a single batch around April of the FOLLOWING year (the 2025 season landed in April 2026) and a live query for the current calendar year returns zero perimeters, so a fire that burned this point months ago still reads as no burn. Taken together: "no recorded burn" is NOT "never burned", and this field can say nothing whatsoever about the current fire season. THE SEARCH IS CAPPED AT 8,000 m — an absent value means "no recorded CAL FIRE FRAP perimeter within 8,000 m of this point", never "no fire anywhere near" and never an unbounded nearest-perimeter distance. Candidate geometry is fetched server-generalized for latency (a full-precision query measured 28.6 s against 0.51 s generalized), which leaves roughly 50 to 100 m of boundary tolerance. Containment and any generalized distance within 150 m of the boundary are now confirmed by an automatic full-precision refetch that recomputes both distance and containment before the value is served, so near-boundary answers ARE decisive; the same refetch also fires near the 1,600 m decision line. Outside both bands the 50-to-100 m tolerance still applies to this mid-range distance: trivial against the 8,000 m cap, but not precise enough to be read to the metre. This is a distance to the perimeter POLYGON boundary — not to the fire's ignition point, and not to any structure: a fire that ignited 20 km away but whose burned area grew to within 200 m of the point correctly reports about 200 m. A perimeter is not burn severity: CAL FIRE documents that over-generalization, particularly on large old fires, shows unburned "islands" inside a final perimeter as burned, so a 0 here does not mean this point itself burned. Prescribed burns are excluded (they live in CAL FIRE's separate rxburn service), so absence here is not absence of fire on the ground; an escaped prescribed burn (CAUSE 18) IS included, correctly, because it became a real uncontrolled wildfire. Duplicate and overlapping perimeters for the same ground are common and normal, so the nearest perimeter is not necessarily the only fire at that distance. ALWAYS read with most_recent_burn_year: both fields are taken from the SAME governing perimeter (or, inside a perimeter, the same containing set), so they can never describe different ground. THE PAIR HAS ONE KNOWN PATHOLOGY and it bites this use case directly: because the year describes the NEAREST perimeter, a 1954 perimeter at 200 m alongside a 2020 perimeter at 900 m reports 1954 — the nearer, older fire — and the 2020 burn is invisible. This field pair alone therefore does NOT settle the compound claim "no recorded burn within X metres since year Y" and is not sufficient evidence for a 10 CCR 2644.9(i) filing resting on that claim; the honest workaround is one extra year-filtered query against the same CAL FIRE layer, asking whether ANY perimeter at or after your cutoff year falls within your radius. CALIFORNIA-ONLY: null outside California means the product does not exist there, never that there is no wildfire history. This is the OBSERVED-history leg of wildfire risk only — pair it with fire_hazard_severity_zone_class and fire_hazard_responsibility_area for the REGULATORY leg (CAL FIRE's Fire Hazard Severity Zones) and with wildfire_annual_frequency for the MODELLED leg (FEMA National Risk Index annualized wildfire frequency, tract level).
fields.name: nearest_fire_perimeter_distance_m
fields.null_meaning: Null in three distinguishable cases, told apart by the field's status plus its provenance note. ABSENT / outside California: CAL FIRE FRAP is a California-only product and does not apply — this is "not applicable", never "no wildfire history". ABSENT / inside California with no perimeter within the 8,000 m search cap: this is a REAL ANSWER — no CAL FIRE FRAP-recorded perimeter within 8,000 m of the point — and it is the closest this field comes to supporting "no recorded burn nearby", but it remains bounded by the cap AND by every completeness caveat in the hints (below-threshold fires, submission gaps, the always-absent current fire season), so it is never "never burned" and never "no fire anywhere near". FAILED: the CAL FIRE query errored, timed out, or returned an unusable payload — no answer was obtained, a retry may help, and a FAILED here must never be read as an absence of burn history. One legitimate divergence to expect: when the governing perimeter carries a null YEAR_, most_recent_burn_year is ABSENT while this distance is still known and valid — the two fields differ in status without disagreeing about which perimeter they describe.

fields.description: Burn year of the governing CAL FIRE FRAP historical wildfire perimeter at the queried point: the most recent year among ALL perimeters containing the point when the point is inside one, otherwise the year of the single geometrically nearest perimeter within the 8,000 m search cap (Firep25_1, fires 1878 through 2025). California-only.
fields.interpretation_hints: The burn year of the governing CAL FIRE FRAP wildfire perimeter, read live from CAL FIRE's own published layer (Firep25_1, released April 2026, 23,334 perimeters, fires 1878 through 2025). Inside a perimeter this is the MAXIMUM year across every perimeter containing the point, because reburns are common and the containing set is often more than one; outside, it is the year of the single geometrically NEAREST perimeter, whose distance is nearest_fire_perimeter_distance_m. The two fields are always taken from the SAME governing perimeter or the same containing set, so they can never disagree about which fire they describe. Near a perimeter boundary, containment itself is confirmed by the same automatic full-precision refetch described on nearest_fire_perimeter_distance_m before this governing perimeter or containing set is chosen, so a near-boundary nearest-vs-containing split resolves to the correct one rather than a generalized guess. READ THE THREE COMPLETENESS FACTS BEFORE YOU READ THE NUMBER, because a false "no burn" is the expensive error with this dataset. FIRST, below-threshold fires are simply absent by design: CAL FIRE's own stated collection criteria are perimeters of 10 acres or more in timber, 50 acres or more in brush, or 300 acres or more in grass, and/or 3 or more impacted residential or commercial structures, and/or 1 or more fatality, with all cooperating agencies submitting at 10 acres or more — a small fire that burned this exact parcel and cleared none of those gates was never collected at all. SECOND, coverage depends on voluntary agency submission, and CAL FIRE states outright that fires are missing because historical records were lost or damaged, documentation was inadequate, or they "have not yet been incorporated into the database" — the gaps are real and are not uniformly distributed. THIRD, and most dangerous for any recency claim, the current fire season is always missing: a season is published in a single batch around April of the FOLLOWING year (the 2025 season landed in April 2026) and a live query for the current calendar year returns zero perimeters, so a fire that burned this point months ago still reads as no burn. Consequence, stated plainly: this field can honestly support "no CAL FIRE FRAP-recorded burn since year Y" only for a Y at or before last calendar year, never for the current season, and "no recorded burn" is NOT "never burned". THE PAIR HAS ONE KNOWN PATHOLOGY, stated loudly because it bites the appeal use case directly: outside a perimeter this year describes the NEAREST perimeter, not the most recent perimeter in range. A 1954 perimeter at 200 m sitting alongside a 2020 perimeter at 900 m reports 1954 — the nearer, older fire — and the 2020 burn is invisible in this field. Therefore this field pair alone does NOT settle the compound claim "no recorded burn within X metres since year Y", because a newer fire slightly farther away is never surfaced, and it is not sufficient evidence for a 10 CCR 2644.9(i) filing resting on that claim; the honest workaround is one extra year-filtered query against the same CAL FIRE layer, asking whether ANY perimeter with a year at or after your cutoff falls within your radius. Data quirks that matter: the year is null on 77 of the 23,334 perimeters, a genuine missing year with no zero sentinel, so the year can be absent while the distance is known; duplicate and overlapping perimeters for the same ground are common and normal (BIG/1900 and LAS FLORES NO. 57/1935 carry identical geometry and identical acreage, and three perimeters from 1979, 1993 and 2025 stack near Eaton), so this year is a property of one governing record, not a count of distinct fires. A perimeter is not burn severity — CAL FIRE documents unburned "islands" inside final perimeters, especially on large old fires — so a year here does not mean this specific point burned in that year, and the value describes the perimeter POLYGON, not the fire's ignition point. Prescribed burns are excluded (separate rxburn service), so absence here is not absence of fire on the ground, while an escaped prescribed burn (CAUSE 18) IS included because it became a real uncontrolled wildfire. CALIFORNIA-ONLY: null outside California means the product does not exist there, never that there is no wildfire history. This is the OBSERVED-history leg of wildfire risk only — pair it with fire_hazard_severity_zone_class and fire_hazard_responsibility_area for the REGULATORY leg and with wildfire_annual_frequency for the MODELLED leg (FEMA National Risk Index annualized wildfire frequency, tract level).
fields.name: most_recent_burn_year
fields.null_meaning: Null in four distinguishable cases, told apart by the field's status plus its provenance note. ABSENT / outside California: CAL FIRE FRAP is a California-only product and does not apply — "not applicable", never "no wildfire history". ABSENT / inside California with no perimeter within the 8,000 m search cap: a REAL ANSWER — no CAL FIRE FRAP-recorded burn within 8,000 m of the point — subject to every completeness caveat in the hints (below-threshold fires, submission gaps, the always-absent current fire season) and bounded by that cap; nearest_fire_perimeter_distance_m is absent for the same reason, so the pair agrees. ABSENT / the governing perimeter exists but its YEAR_ is null (77 of the 23,334 perimeters): the burn year is genuinely unrecorded upstream. This is a semantic absence, NOT a failure, and it is the one case where the two fields legitimately diverge in status — nearest_fire_perimeter_distance_m is still a known, valid distance to that same perimeter, so read the distance and treat the year as unknown, never as no burn. FAILED: the CAL FIRE query errored, timed out, or returned an unusable payload — no answer was obtained and a retry may help; a FAILED year must never be read as an absence of burn history.

fields.description: Fraction (0.0-1.0) of the matched Regrid parcel's own boundary encumbered by PAD-US conservation easement polygons — the parcel share, computed by intersecting easements with the parcel boundary in the parcel's local UTM (equal-area) projection. NOT the whole mapped easement polygon's size (see easement_acres for that).
fields.interpretation_hints: A conservation easement permanently restricts development on the land it covers, so this is a hard buildability constraint, not a risk score. This is the PARCEL SHARE (PAD-US easement ∩ Regrid parcel boundary), distinct from easement_acres, which reports the whole polygon regardless of parcel. 0.0 is a real 'no easement on this parcel' answer, distinct from null (no Regrid parcel matched at this coordinate, or its boundary geometry was unusable). PAD-US is a compiled national inventory, not a title search — it does not capture every recorded easement, and absence here is not evidence of clear title. On a small parcel a small nonzero fraction can sit near the source's mapping resolution; treat it as directional and corroborate with a title search before it is load-bearing.
fields.name: easement_fraction_of_parcel
fields.null_meaning: No Regrid parcel at this coordinate.

fields.description: Absolute acres of PAD-US conservation easement area intersecting the matched Regrid parcel's own boundary — the parcel-clipped encumbered acreage, computed in the parcel's local UTM (equal-area) projection. NOT the whole mapped easement polygon's size (see easement_acres for that).
fields.interpretation_hints: A conservation easement permanently restricts development on the land it covers, so these acres are a hard buildability constraint, not a risk score. This is the PARCEL SHARE (PAD-US easement ∩ Regrid parcel boundary), distinct from easement_acres, which reports the whole polygon regardless of parcel — a large easement can report thousands of acres there while only a sliver falls on this parcel. Pair with parcel_area_m2 to express it as usable land remaining. 0.0 is a real 'no easement on this parcel' answer, distinct from null (no Regrid parcel matched at this coordinate). PAD-US is a compiled national inventory, not a title search — absence is not evidence of clear title.
fields.name: easement_acres_on_parcel
fields.null_meaning: No Regrid parcel at this coordinate.

fields.description: EIA-860 sector of the nearest power plant — one of "Electric Utility", "IPP Non-CHP", "IPP CHP", "Commercial CHP", "Commercial Non-CHP", "Industrial CHP", "Industrial Non-CHP". EIA classifies a generator by its operator's primary line of business, not by whether it physically exports to the grid.
fields.interpretation_hints: READ THIS BEFORE quoting any other nearest_power_plant_* field. Electric Utility / IPP CHP / IPP Non-CHP are EIA's electric power sector — the operator's business IS selling electricity, so these are grid generation. Commercial * / Industrial * generate primarily for their host site: that class spans an office tower's on-site engine, a university cogeneration plant, and an 890 MW refinery combined cycle that exports heavily, so it is NOT a synonym for behind-the-meter backup — judge with nearest_power_plant_capacity_mw + nearest_power_plant_technology. Roughly half of major-US-downtown coordinates return a commercial/industrial plant as nearest, so an urban "nearest power plant" answer that does not state the sector is misleading. Mireye deliberately does NOT filter these out: no capacity, prime-mover or sector rule separates on-site from grid generation without deleting real plants (856 Electric Utility plants are under 5 MW; the largest commercial installation is 99.6 MW). Not a claim about grid export, interconnection capacity or power availability.
fields.name: nearest_power_plant_sector
fields.null_meaning: No EIA plant within the plants search radius, or the EIA sector attribute is blank for the nearest plant.

fields.description: Geodesic distance to the OPEN SEA, where open sea means the water still connected to the deep ocean once every entrance narrower than 20 km is sealed - that is, what lies outside the continental landmass. Bays, sounds, estuaries and tidal rivers are INSIDE that boundary, not part of it, so Baltimore Inner Harbor reads about 139 km and Philadelphia about 90 km even though both sit on tidal water. Points on the outer coast read metres (Santa Monica 40 m, Virginia Beach 450 m, Galveston 890 m). This is NOT the same question as coast_distance_m, which measures to the nearest tidal shoreline of any kind and is the right field for river frontage, port access or tidal exposure; at a bay head the two differ by 100 km or more and both are correct. Returns 0 for a point already in open water, and a large distance rather than a null for an inland point (about 1,365 km in Denver). Great Lakes shoreline is not open sea under this definition and is excluded by construction, since the source ocean polygon contains no lakes. Coverage is the US and its offshore approaches, not the whole coordinate envelope: the open-sea polygon is derived over five processing domains covering about 69 percent of the accepted envelope, and every US shoreline sits inside them (asserted at build time). Outside them - the open North Pacific west of 135W below 46N, and north of 56N - the field is ABSENT rather than a number, because out there the polygon's nearest edge is where a processing box clipped the geometry rather than a coastline, and a distance to that edge would be fiction. No US site is affected.
fields.interpretation_hints: The honest input for hurricane, storm-surge, salt-spray and marine-exposure reasoning, where fronting the open Atlantic and sitting at the head of the Chesapeake are completely different risks. Read it ALONGSIDE coast_distance_m, not instead of it: small coast_distance_m with large open_ocean_distance_m is the signature of sheltered inland tidal water - navigable access, barge and port logistics, low direct marine exposure - while both small means true open-coast exposure. Precision caveat - the boundary is derived from a 1:10m coastline and smoothed by the 10 km sealing radius, so treat this as answering which side of the coastline a site is on rather than as a survey-grade distance. One known artefact of that smoothing: a site inside a coastal concavity narrower than about 20 km reads too far, measured at about 1.3 km in the crook of Cape Cod.
fields.name: open_ocean_distance_m
fields.null_meaning: One of three things, all honest rather than a data gap. Either the coordinate lies OUTSIDE the five processing domains the open-sea polygon is derived over (the open North Pacific west of 135W below 46N, and north of 56N) - out there the polygon's nearest edge is a processing-box clip rather than a coastline, so no distance is reported; or the response was cached before this field existed (terrain responses carry a one-year TTL, so a pre-deploy cache entry reports absent until it expires); or the boundary artifact was unavailable to the serving process. A null NEVER means "no ocean nearby": every coordinate inside the processing domains gets a number - a point in open water returns 0 and a genuinely inland point returns a large distance - and every US shoreline is inside them, asserted at build time. So a null on a US site is a cache or artifact condition, never a coverage one.
